body:
Elements and their classification

An element is a pure substance consisting of only one kind of atom. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical methods. Iron, copper, oxygen, carbon and gold are examples of elements.

Elements differ in their physical properties, such as appearance, hardness and electrical conductivity. They also differ in their chemical behaviour, including how they react with oxygen, water and acids. These differences allow elements to be classified into metals, non-metals and metalloids.

Metals

Metals generally have a shining surface, conduct heat and electricity, and can be shaped into sheets or wires. Examples include iron (Fe), copper (Cu), aluminium (Al), zinc (Zn), silver (Ag) and gold (Au).

Many useful properties of metals are connected. Copper conducts electricity and can be drawn into wires, making it suitable for electrical wiring. Aluminium is relatively light, conducts heat and can be shaped into sheets, making it useful for cooking utensils and foil. Iron is widely used for structures and machinery because of its strength, particularly when used in suitable alloys.

Non-metals

Non-metals generally lack metallic lustre, do not conduct electricity well and cannot be drawn into wires or hammered into sheets. Carbon (C), sulphur (S), oxygen (O), nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and chlorine (Cl) are examples.

Non-metals perform essential functions. Oxygen supports respiration and combustion. Nitrogen and phosphorus are important components of plant nutrients. Chlorine compounds are used in water disinfection. Carbon occurs in substances ranging from graphite to diamond.

Metalloids

Metalloids show a combination of metallic and non-metallic characteristics. Silicon and boron are familiar examples. Silicon is not classified as a metal merely because it sometimes conducts electricity; its overall properties are different from those of ordinary metals.

Physical and chemical properties

A physical property can be observed without changing the substance into a different substance. Lustre, density, malleability, state and conductivity are physical properties.

A chemical property describes how a substance reacts to form new substances. For example, iron can form rust in moist air, whereas gold is much less reactive under ordinary conditions.

The usual physical characteristics help identify metals and non-metals, but they are not absolute rules. Some non-metals are shiny, some metals are soft, and certain non-metals conduct electricity. Chemical behaviour provides additional evidence for classification.

Prelims focus

  • An element contains only one kind of atom.
  • Iron, copper, aluminium and gold are metals.
  • Carbon, sulphur, oxygen and chlorine are non-metals.
  • Silicon and boron are metalloids.
  • Trap: A substance is not necessarily a metal simply because it is shiny or conducts electricity.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 4, Materials: Metals and Non-Metals, pp. 44–47; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, pp. 37–40.]

title: Understanding Metals, Non-metals and Their Classification

body:
How metals and non-metals usually differ

Physical properties explain why different elements are selected for different purposes. However, words such as generally and usually matter because important exceptions exist.

PropertyMetals generallyNon-metals generally
AppearanceHave metallic lustreAppear dull
MalleabilityCan form sheetsBreak rather than flatten
DuctilityCan form wiresCannot form wires
Heat conductionConduct heat wellConduct heat poorly
Electrical conductionConduct electricity wellConduct electricity poorly
SonorityProduce a ringing soundAre generally not sonorous
Physical stateUsually solidMay be solid or gas

Malleability and ductility are different

Malleability is the ability of a material to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets without breaking. Aluminium foil and thin gold sheets demonstrate malleability.

Ductility is the ability of a material to be drawn into thin wires. Copper electrical wires demonstrate ductility.

Gold and silver are exceptionally malleable, while gold is the most ductile metal. Both properties concern the ability to change shape without breaking, but sheets and wires are not the same product.

Lustre, hardness and sonority

Metallic lustre is the characteristic shine of a freshly exposed metal surface. An old metal object may appear dull because its surface has reacted with air. Removing the surface coating can reveal the underlying metallic shine.

Most familiar metals are hard, but hardness varies considerably. Sodium, potassium and lithium are soft metals. A material's hardness alone therefore cannot establish whether it is metallic.

A sonorous material produces a ringing sound when struck. This property explains why many bells are made from metals or metal alloys.

Conductivity and practical uses

Metals conduct electricity because they contain mobile electrons capable of carrying electric charge. Copper and aluminium are widely used in electrical conductors. The conductor in an electrical cable is commonly covered with an insulating material to reduce the risk of electric shock.

Silver and copper are excellent conductors of heat. Aluminium also transfers heat effectively, which helps explain its use in cooking vessels. Lead and mercury are comparatively poor conductors of heat among metals.

Exceptions that change the answer

ElementClassificationImportant exception
MercuryMetalLiquid at ordinary room temperature
BromineNon-metalLiquid at ordinary room temperature
IodineNon-metalHas a lustrous appearance
GraphiteNon-metallic form of carbonConducts electricity
DiamondNon-metallic form of carbonExtremely hard
Sodium and potassiumMetalsSoft enough to be cut with a knife
Gallium and caesiumMetalsHave unusually low melting points

Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element. Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon. Diamond is exceptionally hard, whereas graphite conducts electricity. Their different structures produce different physical properties even though both consist of carbon atoms.

Mercury is the familiar exception to the rule that metals are solid at room temperature. Gallium and caesium melt at temperatures only slightly above typical room temperature, but they are not generally liquid under ordinary room conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Malleability means formation of sheets; ductility means formation of wires.
  • Gold is exceptionally ductile; gold and silver are exceptionally malleable.
  • Mercury is a liquid metal; bromine is a liquid non-metal at room temperature.
  • Iodine is lustrous, graphite conducts electricity, and diamond is very hard.
  • Trap: Graphite is not a metal even though it conducts electricity.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Section 3.1, pp. 37–40; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 4, Materials: Metals and Non-Metals, pp. 44–46.]

title: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals: Rules and Exceptions

body:
What happens when elements combine with oxygen?

When an element reacts with oxygen, it may form an oxide. Metals generally form metal oxides, while non-metals form non-metal oxides. The chemical nature of the oxide gives useful information about the element and its reactions.

Basic metal oxides

Most metal oxides are basic oxides. They react with acids to form a salt and water. Some basic metal oxides also react with water to form metal hydroxides.

Magnesium burns in oxygen with a bright white flame and forms magnesium oxide:

2Mg + O2 → 2MgO

Magnesium oxide is basic. It reacts with water to produce magnesium hydroxide:

MgO + H2O → Mg(OH)2

When copper is heated in air, its reddish-brown surface develops a black coating of copper(II) oxide:

2Cu + O2 → 2CuO

The black coating is evidence of a chemical reaction. The copper has formed a new substance rather than merely changing shape.

Acidic non-metal oxides

Many non-metals form acidic oxides. These react with bases to produce salts and water. Some form acids when they react with water.

Sulphur burns in oxygen to form sulphur dioxide:

S + O2 → SO2

Sulphur dioxide can react with water to form sulphurous acid:

SO2 + H2O → H2SO3

Carbon dioxide is another acidic non-metal oxide. However, not every non-metal oxide is acidic: carbon monoxide (CO) is an example of a neutral oxide.

Amphoteric metal oxides

An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and bases. Two important examples are aluminium oxide (Al2O3) and zinc oxide (ZnO).

For example, aluminium oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to form aluminium chloride and water:

Al2O3 + 6HCl → 2AlCl3 + 3H2O

It also reacts with sodium hydroxide, producing sodium aluminate and water:

Al2O3 + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO2 + H2O

Thus, the statement that all metal oxides are basic is incorrect. Most are basic, while some are amphoteric.

Why different metals behave differently in air

Potassium and sodium react very rapidly with oxygen and moisture. Their high reactivity is why they are kept under kerosene rather than exposed to air.

Aluminium forms a thin, tightly attached layer of aluminium oxide when exposed to air. This layer slows further reaction and helps protect the metal. The presence of an oxide coating does not always mean that the underlying metal will continue to corrode rapidly.

Silver and gold do not readily combine with oxygen, even at high temperatures under ordinary textbook conditions. Their low reactivity helps explain why they are valued for jewellery and decorative articles.

Oxide formation and corrosion are related but not identical ideas. A stable, protective oxide layer on aluminium can slow further attack, whereas the flaky rust formed on iron does not provide similarly effective protection.

Prelims focus

  • Magnesium oxide is basic.
  • Sulphur dioxide is an acidic non-metal oxide.
  • Aluminium oxide and zinc oxide are amphoteric.
  • Heated copper forms black copper(II) oxide.
  • Aluminium develops a protective oxide layer.
  • Trap: Not all metal oxides are exclusively basic, and not all non-metal oxides are acidic.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Sections 3.1–3.2.1, pp. 40–42; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 4, Materials: Metals and Non-Metals, pp. 46–48.]

title: Chemical Reactions with Oxygen and the Nature of Oxides

body:
Why different metals react differently with water

Metals do not all react with water at the same rate. Some react vigorously with cold water, some require hot water or steam, and others show no reaction with water under these conditions. These differences are closely related to the metals' reactivity.

MetalsConditionsUsual observation
Potassium, sodiumCold waterVery vigorous reaction; hydrogen and metal hydroxide form
CalciumCold waterLess vigorous reaction; hydrogen and calcium hydroxide form
MagnesiumHot waterReacts to form magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen
Aluminium, zinc, ironSteamReact under suitable conditions to form metal oxides and hydrogen
Lead, copper, silver, goldWater or steamNo ordinary reaction

Sodium reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide and hydrogen:

2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2

The reaction releases considerable heat. In the case of sodium and potassium, the hydrogen produced may ignite.

Calcium also reacts with cold water:

Ca + 2H2O → Ca(OH)2 + H2

Calcium may appear to float because bubbles of hydrogen stick to its surface. Floating is therefore not evidence that calcium is less dense than water.

Iron does not react appreciably with cold water in the same manner as sodium. It reacts with steam under suitable conditions:

3Fe + 4H2O → Fe3O4 + 4H2

How metals react with dilute acids

Many metals react with dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulphuric acid to form a salt and hydrogen gas. A general school-level relationship is:

Reactive metal + dilute acid → salt + hydrogen

For example:

Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2

Fe + H2SO4 → FeSO4 + H2

Hydrogen is a combustible gas. The characteristic popping sound associated with its ignition is a familiar identification fact.

However, copper does not release hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulphuric acid under ordinary conditions. Copper is less reactive than hydrogen and cannot displace it from these acids.

The nitric acid exception

Nitric acid (HNO3) is an oxidising acid. When metals react with it, hydrogen gas is generally not released because the acid oxidises the hydrogen that would otherwise be produced. School-level exceptions include magnesium and manganese with very dilute nitric acid.

This qualification is important: the statement that every metal-acid reaction releases hydrogen is false.

Reactions with bases

Some metals, notably aluminium and zinc, also react with strong bases under suitable conditions and release hydrogen gas. Such behaviour is consistent with the amphoteric character of their oxides.

It is therefore incorrect to assume that metals react only with acids or that every metal reacts with bases in the same way.

Prelims focus

  • Sodium and potassium react vigorously with cold water.
  • Calcium reacts with cold water; magnesium reacts with hot water.
  • Iron, zinc and aluminium react with steam under suitable conditions.
  • Copper, silver and gold do not ordinarily react with water.
  • Metals above hydrogen generally release hydrogen from dilute HCl or dilute H2SO4.
  • Trap: Nitric acid does not generally follow the ordinary metal-plus-dilute-acid hydrogen rule.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Sections 3.2.2–3.2.3, pp. 42–44; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 4, Materials: Metals and Non-Metals, pp. 48–50.]
